faqs.q: What is High-Level Design (HLD) in a system design interview?
faqs.a: HLD is the architecture-level part of a system design round: you clarify requirements, estimate scale, define APIs and entities, choose databases, caches and queues, draw the end-to-end architecture and then defend the trade-offs and failure handling. This book teaches that flow with 19 worked case studies.

faqs.q: What is the difference between HLD and LLD?
faqs.a: HLD answers how a whole system scales: services, data stores, caching, messaging and consistency. LLD answers how one component is built: classes, interfaces, SOLID principles and design patterns. This page covers HLD; the Java-first LLD handbook and an HLD + LLD bundle are linked on this page.

faqs.q: Is this book only for experienced engineers?
faqs.a: No. The page starts from the interview method and core building blocks, then moves into complete case studies. It is especially useful when you already know basic backend development but want a structured HLD approach.

faqs.q: How are the 19 case studies structured?
faqs.a: Each case follows the same sequence: interview prompt, clarifying questions, functional and non-functional requirements, estimation, interviewer expectations, entities, APIs, database design, HLD, request flows, algorithms/deep dives, trade-offs and failures.

faqs.q: Does it cover Redis, Kafka, sharding and distributed systems?
faqs.a: Yes. The case studies repeatedly use API gateways, load balancers, Redis, Kafka, CDC, Elasticsearch, object storage/CDNs, SQL/NoSQL choices, sharding, replication, locks, retries, idempotency and observability in context.

faqs.q: Does the book include BookMyShow-style concurrency problems?
faqs.a: Yes. The ticket-booking case focuses on seat inventory, temporary holds, locking/transactions, payment state transitions, timeout release and flash-sale traffic.
